topic_and_scope: A critical analysis of wheat metabolomics in the context of abiotic and biotic stress tolerance, highlighting how integration with other omics and emerging technologies can enhance breeding. The focus is on translating metabolite knowledge into mechanistic insights and field-relevant improvements.
main_themes: Multiomics integration to map resistance mechanisms and metabolite regulation in wheat
Advances in metabolomics technologies (spatial, flux, single-cell) and their application to wheat
Pathways from metabolite discovery to breeding and field deployment (biomarkers, validated targets, and breeding tools)
main_findings: Wheat metabolomics has identified key osmoprotectants and defense metabolites (e.g., proline, polyamines, flavonoids, phenolics, lipids) that correlate with drought, cold, salinity, and disease resistance.

Meta-analyses and integrated mQTL/mGWAS approaches have begun to link metabolites to specific genomic regions and candidate resistance genes, enabling targeted breeding and genetic modification strategies.

key_gaps.description: Single-cell metabolomics has not yet been applied to wheat; current wheat metabolomics relies on bulk tissue analyses which obscure cellular heterogeneity and compartment-specific metabolism.
Limited understanding of wheat metabolic regulatory networks due to genome complexity and fragmented pathway annotation, hindering mechanistic interpretation of stress responses.
Insufficient wheat-specific metabolite databases and reference metabolome coverage; public resources cover only a fraction of plant metabolites, constraining annotation and biomarker discovery.

future_directions.title: Develop and apply single-cell metabolomics in wheat
future_directions.rationale: The field explicitly notes that single-cell metabolomics has not yet been utilized in wheat. Establishing workflows for cell isolation, ionization, and detection in wheat tissues (leaves, roots, grains) will reveal cellular heterogeneity and subcellular compartmentalization of stress metabolites. Concrete steps include adapting nano-ESI, LAESI, or SIMS approaches for wheat tissues, creating cell-type–specific metabolite maps, and integrating with single-cell transcriptomics for multi-layer networks.

future_directions.title: Implement spatial metabolomics to map metabolite distributions in wheat tissues under stress
future_directions.rationale: Spatial metabolomics is highlighted as a promising approach to localize metabolites within tissues and cells. Applying DESI or MALDI imaging to drought-, cold-, salinity-, and pathogen-exposed wheat organs (leaves, stems, kernels) will link metabolite localization to function and resistance loci. Steps include developing wheat-specific tissue preparation protocols, building spatial metabolite atlases under key stresses, and integrating with histology and transcriptomics.

future_directions.title: Establish wheat metabolic fluxomics using isotopic tracers
future_directions.rationale: Fluxomics provides dynamic insight into pathway activities, which is critical for understanding how stresses rewire metabolism. Implement 13C/15N labeling in hydroponic or soil-based systems to monitor real-time carbon and nitrogen fluxes in core pathways (Calvin cycle, amino acid biosynthesis) under stress. Combine GC-MS/LC-MS with flux balance modeling and integrate with transcriptomic data to map regulatory control points.

future_directions.title: Expand mQTL/mGWAS mapping for metabolites under abiotic and biotic stresses in diverse wheat germplasm
future_directions.rationale: mQTL/mGWAS approaches have begun to link metabolites to genomic regions, but broader, high-resolution mapping across diverse genotypes and stress conditions is needed. Actions include assembling large, diverse panels, standardized metabolomic profiling under controlled and field conditions, and validating candidate genes via gene editing or overexpression. This will yield robust metabolite-associated markers for breeding.

future_directions.title: Integrate multiomics to identify resistance pathways and validate candidate genes in wheat
future_directions.rationale: The review emphasizes multiomics as a powerful approach for deciphering resistance mechanisms. Implement integrated pipelines combining genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics in NILs or diverse lines under specific stresses, followed by network analyses and functional validation (CRISPR/Cas, overexpression). The goal is to move from correlation to causation for key metabolites and their biosynthetic genes.

future_directions.title: Build and curate wheat-specific metabolite databases and semi-annotated metabolomics pipelines
future_directions.rationale: Public databases cover a small fraction of plant metabolites; expanding wheat-specific metabolite coverage is essential for accurate annotation and biomarker discovery. Actions include large-scale, tissue- and stress-specific metabolome profiling, development of semi-annotated metabolomics workflows, and establishing community-curated wheat metabolite reference libraries accessible to breeders and researchers.

future_directions.title: Conduct field-relevant exogenous metabolite screening to enhance stress tolerance across genotypes
future_directions.rationale: Exogenous application of selective chemicals has been proposed to screen for tolerance; translating this to field conditions across diverse genotypes will identify practical protective compounds and potentiation strategies. Steps involve controlled field trials applying candidate metabolites (e.g., proline, glycine betaine, flavonoids) and measuring yield, quality, and stress indicators across multiple environments.

future_directions.title: Translate metabolomics findings into breeding programs using metabolite-informed markers
future_directions.rationale: To realize impact, metabolomic insights must feed breeding pipelines. This includes developing metabolite-based markers, integrating them into marker-assisted selection and genomic selection models, and validating performance under realistic stress scenarios. Pilot breeding programs should couple metabolomics readouts with phenotypic germplasm evaluation to ensure yield and resilience gains in the field.
